idiom_name: publisher + subscription registry + per-subscriber copy queue
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the publisher calls one publish(topic, message) entry point; the channel keeps a subscription registry (topic or event type to subscriber) and, per publish, copies the immutable message once into each subscription's own queue or invokes each subscriber. The delivery contract must be designed explicitly: subscription durability (transient vs durable), per-subscriber ordering, overflow policy for slow consumers (block, drop-oldest, disconnect), and message retention. The dispatcher iterates over a snapshot of the registry so subscribers can attach or detach while a publish is in flight, and subscribers must never share mutable message state.
code_sketch:
channel.subscribe(topic, subscriber)      # one queue per subscriber
channel.publish(topic, message)
for sub in channel.snapshot(topic):      # snapshot, then dispatch outside the lock
    sub.enqueue(copy_of(message))        # bounded queue + declared overflow policy
# each subscriber drains its own queue on its own thread;
# durable subscriptions persist the queue, transient ones discard on detach
pitfalls: Handing one mutable message instance to every subscriber aliases state across them; freeze or copy the payload per subscription.
No overflow policy for slow subscribers: the publisher either blocks permanently or drops messages silently.
Mutating the subscription registry from inside a callback; dispatch must run over a snapshot taken before the calls.

Wrong move: Put every downstream application in one Kafka consumer group -> delivery is load-balanced within the group, so each application does not receive every record -> instead assign each independent reaction its own consumer group.
Wrong move: Treat broker fan-out as exactly-once side effects -> retries and redelivery can repeat a subscriber's work -> instead make handlers idempotent and use acknowledgements or deduplication.

Wrong move: Give every subscriber an unfiltered view of a broad topic -> unrelated consumers receive data they should not see and coupling grows -> instead apply per-subscription filters or split least-privilege topics.
